identification.summary: China-linked cyber espionage group that Microsoft tracks as Canary Typhoon and maps to BlackTech, Palmerworm, CIRCUIT PANDA and APT24 [S1]. Trend Micro first described BlackTech in 2017, linking the PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow and Waterbear campaigns to one group operating against East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally Japan and Hong Kong [S2]. A September 2023 US-Japan joint advisory warned that BlackTech modifies router firmware and abuses trust between subsidiary and headquarters networks to pivot into targets in Japan and the US [S7][S8]. Trend Micro reported in 2024 that the group (tracked as Earth Hundun) continued to develop Waterbear and its successor Deuterbear against technology and government organizations in Asia-Pacific [S9][S10].
identification.firstObserved: Trend Micro (2017): PLEAD active since 2012, with secondary reporting placing Shrouded Crossbow activity as early as 2010 [S2]. Symantec states the group has been active since at least 2013 [S5]. Trend Micro reports Waterbear versions dating back to 2009 [S9].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Canary Typhoon. Microsoft's public mapping lists CIRCUIT PANDA, APT24, Palmerworm and BlackTech for Canary Typhoon and gives no former DEV/element name; no Microsoft blog post describing Canary Typhoon activity was found [S1]. Cluster caution: Microsoft maps APT24 to Canary Typhoon [S1], but Google Threat Intelligence Group equates APT24 with Pitty Tiger (MITRE G0011, separate from BlackTech G0098) and assesses it as closely related to Earth Aughisky [S11]. This profile is built on BlackTech/Palmerworm/Earth Hundun reporting; APT24/Pitty Tiger activity (e.g., GTIG's 2025 BADAUDIO report) is kept out of the campaign timeline. The joint advisory lists Palmerworm, Temp.Overboard, Circuit Panda and Radio Panda as BlackTech aliases [S7].

attribution.sponsor: People's Republic of China. The US-Japan joint advisory describes BlackTech as 'People's Republic of China-linked cyber actors' [S7][S8]. Symantec notes Taiwanese officials have publicly stated they believe the group is backed by the Chinese government [S5].
attribution.confidence: Government: NSA, FBI, CISA, Japan's National Police Agency and NISC jointly link BlackTech to the PRC (September 2023) [S7]. Microsoft places Canary Typhoon in its China ('Typhoon') family [S1]. Symantec did not itself attribute Palmerworm to a specific country in its 2020 report [S5]. No public indictment or named sponsoring agency (MSS/PLA) was found.
attribution.basis: Joint government advisory on router-firmware tradecraft [S7][S8]; Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]; long-running vendor reporting from Trend Micro, ESET, Symantec, NTT and others tying shared C2 infrastructure and malware families together [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S9].

objectives: Long-term cyber espionage and information theft [S5]. Trend Micro assessed from C2 mutexes and domain names that the campaigns are likely designed to steal targets' technology, and PLEAD shows a penchant for confidential documents [S2]. NTT reporting describes technology theft against Japanese and Hong Kong firms alongside a Taiwan focus [S6]. The joint advisory highlights access to entities supporting the US and Japanese militaries [S7].

sectors: Entities supporting the US and Japanese militaries / defense industrial base [S7]
Finance, engineering and construction (2019-2020 Palmerworm campaign) [S5]
targeting.notes: The 2023 advisory describes BlackTech compromising branch or overseas-subsidiary routers to pivot into headquarters networks in Japan and the US, so multinational corporations with East Asian subsidiaries are exposed even when the parent is outside the region [S7][S8]. Sector lists differ slightly between the advisory text (government, industrial, technology, media, electronics, telecommunications, entities supporting US and Japanese militaries) and the CISA press release (which cites the defense industrial base); this wording comes from secondary reporting [S7].

capabilities.summary: Custom, regularly retooled malware: PLEAD backdoor and DRIGO exfiltration tool, KIVARS and Waterbear (secondary backdoor installed after privilege is gained) [S2]; Consock, Waship, Dalwit and Nomri backdoors plus dual-use and living-off-the-land tools in 2019-2020 [S5]; Flagpro downloader, SelfMake Loader and Spider RAT from 2020-2021 [S6]; BendyBear and FakeDead cited in the 2023 advisory [S7]; and Deuterbear, a Waterbear successor first seen in October 2022 with anti-memory-scanning, shellcode plugins and HTTPS C2 [S9][S10]. Waterbear is described by Trend Micro as having more than ten versions since 2009 with extensive anti-debug and anti-sandbox features [S9]. Code signing with stolen certificates from D-Link and Changing Information Technology to sign PLEAD and a password stealer (2018) [S3]. Probable router-level man-in-the-middle abuse of the ASUS WebStorage update process to deliver PLEAD (2019) [S4]. Spear-phishing with password-protected archives containing macro documents impersonating business partners [S6]. Network-device tradecraft: after gaining admin access (typically stolen credentials), modifying Cisco router firmware with an SSH backdoor that hides connections from logs, disabling logging, and exploiting router domain-trust relationships to move from subsidiaries to headquarters; the agencies note the technique is not limited to Cisco [S7][S8]. PLEAD operators were also reported to scan for vulnerable routers and enable their VPN feature to stage C2 or delivery servers [S2].

campaigns.name: PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow and Waterbear linked as BlackTech
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro ties three campaigns to one group via shared C&C infrastructure; PLEAD (active since 2012) targets Taiwanese government agencies and private organizations through spear-phishing.

campaigns.name: PLEAD signed with stolen Taiwanese certificates
campaigns.summary: ESET reports PLEAD and a password stealer signed with code-signing certificates stolen from D-Link and Changing Information Technology; the certificates were revoked on 3-4 July 2018.

campaigns.name: PLEAD via ASUS WebStorage update abuse
campaigns.summary: ESET observes PLEAD created by the legitimate AsusWSPanel.exe process, mostly in Taiwan, and judges router-level man-in-the-middle the most likely vector.

campaigns.name: Palmerworm campaign
campaigns.summary: Symantec reports espionage against media, electronics and finance firms in Taiwan, an engineering company in Japan and a construction firm in China, with US targeting also noted, using new backdoors and living-off-the-land tools.

campaigns.name: Flagpro phishing against Japanese companies
campaigns.summary: NTT Security reports macro-laden archives impersonating business partners that drop the Flagpro downloader for reconnaissance and second-stage delivery.

campaigns.name: Deuterbear introduced
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro first observes Deuterbear, a distinct successor to Waterbear, used against technology, research and government targets in Asia-Pacific; analysis published April-May 2024.

campaigns.name: US-Japan advisory: PRC-linked actors hide in router firmware
campaigns.summary: NSA, FBI, CISA, NPA and NISC warn that BlackTech modifies router firmware and abuses subsidiary-to-headquarters trust to reach targets in Japan and the US.

diamond.adversary: PRC-linked espionage operators per US and Japanese agencies [S7]; tracked by Microsoft as Canary Typhoon [S1] and by vendors as BlackTech, Palmerworm and Earth Hundun [S2][S5][S9]. No named individuals or sponsoring agency found.
diamond.capability: PLEAD, KIVARS, Waterbear/Deuterbear, Flagpro, BendyBear, FakeDead and other custom families; stolen code-signing certificates; router firmware modification with SSH backdoor [S2][S3][S5][S6][S7][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: C&C servers shared across campaigns; compromised routers with VPN enabled used as C2 or delivery servers; cloud storage used for delivery and exfiltration drop points [S2]; compromised branch and subsidiary routers as pivot points [S7]; HTTPS C2 for Deuterbear [S10].
diamond.victim: Government, technology, electronics, media, telecommunications, industrial and defense-supporting organizations in Taiwan, Japan, Hong Kong, the US and wider Asia-Pacific [S2][S5][S7][S9].
diamond.socioPolitical: Technology and confidential-document theft aligned with PRC interests in Taiwan and Japan, plus access to entities supporting US and Japanese militaries [S2][S6][S7].
diamond.technology: Edge routers and their trust relationships, software update channels without integrity checks (ASUS WebStorage), Windows code-signing trust, and email-borne macro documents [S3][S4][S6][S7].

gaps: No Microsoft Threat Intelligence report describing Canary Typhoon activity was found; the Microsoft link rests only on the public naming mapping [S1].

Microsoft maps APT24 to Canary Typhoon, while Google/Mandiant treats APT24 as Pitty Tiger (MITRE G0011), separate from BlackTech (G0098). The imported alias list also includes Pitty Tiger-related names (Temp.Pittytiger, PITTY PANDA). Whether these clusters are the same actor remains unresolved; APT24 BADAUDIO activity (2022-2025) was not merged [S1][S11].
The primary joint advisory PDF (ic3.gov / cisa.gov) could not be opened; its content is taken from search-result and press coverage [S7][S8].
Primary vendor reports from Trend Micro, ESET, Symantec and NTT could not be fetched directly; details come from search-result summaries and press coverage of those reports.
MITRE ATT&CK G0098 page could not be fetched in this session; technique and software lists come from the imported record.
Initial access method for the router compromises (beyond stolen administrative credentials) and the identity of victims in the 2023 advisory are not public in the sources gathered.
No public indictment, sanctions or identification of the PRC organization behind BlackTech was found.
No public reporting after 2024 specific to BlackTech/Earth Hundun was found in this research pass.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Key cyber terrain includes edge and branch routers connecting East Asian subsidiaries, partner sites and contractors to US and Japanese headquarters networks, since BlackTech pivots along those trust paths [S7]. Defense-supporting organizations in Japan and Taiwan sit inside this environment [S7]. STEP 2 (effects): Firmware-level router persistence with log suppression degrades defenders' visibility and survives host-level remediation; stolen code-signing certificates and hijacked update channels undermine software-trust assumptions [S3][S4][S7]. STEP 3 (adversary template): spear-phishing or stolen credentials, then first-stage downloader (Flagpro/PLEAD), then secondary backdoor (Waterbear/Deuterbear), then document theft; in parallel, admin access to routers, firmware replacement, and lateral movement from subsidiary to headquarters [S2][S6][S7][S9]. STEP 4: MLCOA is persistent technology and document theft from government, technology and defense-supporting entities in Taiwan, Japan and the US [S2][S5][S7]. MDCOA is covert firmware-level control of routers on paths serving US and Japanese military-support networks, positioning the actor to collect or disrupt traffic during a Taiwan Strait crisis (analyst extrapolation; no disruptive activity reported). Candidate indicators: router firmware image hash mismatches, unexpected reboots or image changes, SSH sessions not reflected in logs, outbound VTY connections, logging disabled on network devices, and executables signed with revoked Taiwanese vendor certificates [S3][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: network-device integrity (firmware hashes, configuration drift, logging status) should be a reported data feed, because host EDR alone will not see this actor's router persistence [S7]. (2) Authorities: many affected routers belong to coalition partners, contractors or overseas subsidiaries outside DoDIN control; responses depend on partner and private-sector coordination rather than unilateral action [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: map mission dependencies on links that traverse East Asian partner or subsidiary networks and treat them as potentially compromised; apply zero-trust controls and review subsidiary connections as the advisory recommends [S7]. (4) Coordination: the advisory was co-authored by US and Japanese agencies, so information sharing with Japan's NPA and NISC and with DC3/DIB partners is the natural channel for indicators and remediation status [S7].

provenance.importedSummary: BlackTech is a cyber espionage group operating against targets in East Asia, particularly Taiwan, and occasionally, Japan and Hong Kong. Based on the mutexes and domain names of some of their C&C servers, BlackTech’s campaigns are likely designed to steal their target’s technology. Following their activities and evolving tactics and techniques helped us uncover the proverbial red string of fate that connected three seemingly disparate campaigns: PLEAD, Shrouded Crossbow, and of late, Waterbear. PLEAD is an information theft campaign with a penchant for confidential documents. Active since 2012, it has so far targeted Taiwanese government agencies and private organizations. PLEAD’s toolset includes the self-named PLEAD backdoor and the DRIGO exfiltration tool. PLEAD uses spear-phishing emails to deliver and install their backdoor, either as an attachment or through links to cloud storage services. Some of the cloud storage accounts used to deliver PLEAD are also used as drop off points for exfiltrated documents stolen by DRIGO. PLEAD actors use a router scanner tool to scan for vulnerable routers, after which the attackers will enable the router’s VPN feature then register a machine as virtual server. This virtual server will be used either as a C&C server or an HTTP server that delivers PLEAD malware to their targets.
